Sunlight rests on a tranquil Moroccan medina street recalling Chefchaouen. A tall blue tower house stands as the central landmark, a dark wooden room projecting below its roof. Around it, roughly fifteen to twenty tightly adjoining two- to four-story buildings line both sides of a broad, straight road.

Weathered cobalt and powder blue mingle with white, pale turquoise, dusty coral, and peach stucco; chipped plaster frequently exposes dark stone masonry. Predominantly orange terracotta roof tiles give way here and there to pale-blue tiled pyramidal roofs and flat blue terraces. Recessed courtyards, narrow alleys, horseshoe-arched passages, exterior stair landings, projecting timber galleries, small balconies, and overlapping rooflines layer the irregular façades.

Alternating blue-and-white bands frame deep-set wooden doors and arched windows. Flowering vines, tall palms, twin-lantern streetlights, and occasional wooden benches complete the compact street. Beneath them, worn, slightly reflective paving holds broad shallow puddles between pale raised curbs and narrow dark cobbled sidewalks.
